newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan Q1 GDP surges, but full-year forecast down.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Q1 GDP surges, but full-year forecast down.

text.p: Taiwan on Friday announced a dramatic rise in first quarter gross domestic product growth, but lowered its full-year forecast due to a widespread farm epidemic and a perceived breakdown in law and order.
The government's statistics agency said gross domestic product grew 6.83 percent year-on-year in the first quarter, above the fourth quarter's 6.62 percent annual rise.
"The trend of recovery is getting ever clearer," said a statement issued by the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
The better-than-expected first-quarter rise sharply surpassed an average forecast for a 6.48 percent increase taken from a May 12 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.
Daniel Chen, chief economist of Chinatrust Commercial Bank, cautiously welcomed the figures.
"It is quite a surprise. The first-quarter figure is very, very good," Chen said.

"But we have to keep in mind that first-quarter 1996 was not a very good time," Chen said, referring arch-rival China's sabre rattling in the Taiwan Strait in the run-up to the island's March 1996 presidential election.
"The economy is definitely heading towards a recovery, but I doubt it will be fast growth," he added.

Despite the first-quarter surge, the directorate revised downward its full-year 1997 GDP growth forecast to 6.24 percent from 6.28 percent, saying the devastating farm epidemic that broke out in March would pull second-quarter growth sharply below original projections.

An island-wide outbreak of hog foot and mouth disease has forced Taiwan temporarily to ban all fresh and frozen pork exports -- a US$1.55 billion a year industry -- and to slaughter nearly four million of the island's 14 million hogs.

The statistics agency director Wei Duan said full-year growth also would be negatively affected by a perceived breakdown in law and order in Taiwan, saying this was expected to slow investment due to eroding business confidence.
Ma Kai, research fellow at Chunghua Institution for Economic Research, said the government needed to demonstrate its determination to improve social order.
"Concerns over social order can be removed easily if the government is willing to take effective measures...but the longer it waits, the more damage it will cause," Ma said.
Wei issued the first official GDP forecast for 1998, saying Taiwan's economy was expected to grow 6.26 percent based on current projections.
Taiwan's economy has slowed significantly from its "Asian dragon" days of double-digit growth in the 1980s.

Growth in the mid-1990s has hovered around six percent, but dipped to 5.4 percent in the second half of 1995 -- a time of intense political and military tensions with long-time arch rival communist China.

Helped by a range of government stimulus plans and an easing of frictions with China, GDP growth moved back above six percent in the second half of 1996, but still came in at a disappointing 5.71 percent for all of 1996.
